Research sessions append here; writing sessions read only.

_rules.sourceRequired: a verified tip without a sourceUrl is a bug

tips.mechanism: Low calcium hardness does not cause foam, but it is what lets foam form easily and persist — typically at 150 ppm or below, with 200-300 ppm suppressing it. That makes persistent foam a free readout on the one water imbalance that hides in plain sight: low calcium hardness leaves the water looking sparkling clean rather than cloudy, so nothing about the pool's appearance warns you, while soft corrosive water quietly etches plaster and attacks metal fittings. Owners skim the foam, or wait for the algaecide to wear off, and never test the number the foam was pointing at. Foam that keeps coming back after the organics are oxidised is not a foam problem — it is a calcium hardness reading you have not taken.
tips.appliesTo: Foamy pool water, foam vs bubbles, calcium hardness, soft water, corrosive water, plaster etching
tips.sourceTitle: Discount Salt Pool — Foam vs. Bubbles in Pool Water

tips.mechanism: A teal or blue-green stain in a pool that has never seen a copper algaecide is not really a stain problem. Copper does not arrive on its own, and the most common source is the heater: water held at low pH strips copper from the heat exchanger and carries it into the pool, where it plates onto the plaster. So the stain is an autopsy — it is telling you the inside of the heater has been dissolving, and it is still dissolving now if the pH has not been corrected. Owners treat the plaster, the stain returns in a month, and nobody looks at the heater until it fails. If a teal stain appears and there is a heater on the system, the pH history matters more than the stain remover.
tips.appliesTo: Pool stains, copper, teal or blue-green staining, low pH, heat exchanger, heater corrosion

tips.mechanism: Pollen grains carry a waxy, water-repellent outer coat — it is how they shed moisture in the wild. In a pool that property means pollen clumps and rides on the surface rather than dispersing through the water column, and it is why a skimmer lifts pollen out easily while a filter struggles with it once it sinks. Mustard algae does the opposite: disturb it and it disperses into the water as a plume, because it has no reason to repel water. That gives a reader an identification before touching a brush — riding on the surface in clumps and rafts is pollen; sitting on walls and floor in shaded patches is not.
tips.appliesTo: Yellow dust, mustard algae, pollen, surface film, skimming
tips.sourceTitle: Dog Days Pools — Is That Yellow Stuff in My Pool Mustard Algae or Pollen?

tips.mechanism: Ask what the pool is made of before testing anything. Cyanobacteria needs microscopic surface texture to anchor its holdfasts; a smooth gelcoat or vinyl liner does not offer it. So black spots on a fiberglass pool are usually not algae at all — they are cobalt coming through the gelcoat from underneath, which is why they powder away under a brush and reappear in exactly the same place within days. Owners routinely spend months holding chlorine at 20-30 ppm against something that was never alive, and scratch the gelcoat with a stainless brush while doing it. The surface material narrows the diagnosis before a single test strip comes out of the bottle.
tips.appliesTo: Black spots, black algae, cobalt spotting, fiberglass, gelcoat, vinyl liner
tips.sourceTitle: Fibretech — Black Spots on Pool Surface Explained

tips.mechanism: Calcium does not come out of solution evenly. It crystallizes in the hottest water first — inside the heat exchanger, across salt cell plates, at a sunlit spillway or tile line. Two consequences owners never connect: milky water appearing right after a heater run points at saturation rather than anything added; and if the pool is going milky, the heater and cell are already scaling internally where it cannot be seen. Checking the cell for white crust is a free early warning weeks before the pool itself goes white.
tips.appliesTo: Milky white water, calcium hardness, scale, salt cell, heater
tips.sourceTitle: Orenda Technologies — LSI Balance and Calcium Management (Pillar 1)

tips.mechanism: Water can go cloudy because it is precipitating calcium carbonate rather than holding debris. When pH and calcium hardness climb far enough, carbonate stops staying dissolved and forms microscopic crystals through the water column. Every standard fix fails: filtering cannot outpace crystals forming, clarifier has no debris to gather, and shocking raises pH further and precipitates more. The free diagnostic is timing — filtration problems take days, this appears between one test and the next.
tips.appliesTo: Cloudy water, milky water, cloudy after shocking, new plaster
tips.sourceTitle: Orenda Technologies — What causes cloudy pool water?

tips.mechanism: A suction-side leak pulls air in rather than pushing water out, so it never leaves a puddle. Hunting for water is worse than useless — any water found is on the pressure side and therefore ruled out as the cause of a priming failure. Invert the test: look for bubbles entering the pump lid window and trace where they start.
tips.appliesTo: Pump will not prime, pump loses prime, air in returns
tips.sourceTitle: Inyo Pools — How to Test for Suction Side Air Leaks

tips.mechanism: Failed pump bearings are usually a symptom, not the disease. The mechanical seal wears and weeps, water tracks along the shaft into the motor's front bearing, washes out the grease and corrodes the race. Months later the bearing screeches and everyone calls it a motor fault. Replacing the motor alone puts a new motor behind the same worn seal and buys the same failure twice. The early tell is a drip between wet end and motor that appears while running.
tips.appliesTo: Loud pump, screeching bearings, motor replacement, pump leaking underneath
tips.sourceTitle: Inyo Pools — How To Troubleshoot a Pool Pump Motor: Motor Noisy

tips.mechanism: A pump that dies and works again about half an hour later is not an intermittent electrical fault. It is the motor's built-in thermal overload cutting on heat and reclosing once cool — a reset interval of roughly 20-30 minutes is the characteristic signature. The overload is the alarm, not the fault: something is making the motor run hot (failing bearings adding drag, blocked cooling vents, direct sun, low supply voltage, cavitation). People replace breakers and rewire timers for weeks because the pump runs every time they test it.
tips.appliesTo: Pump not turning on, pump starts then stops, motor overheating, breaker confusion
tips.sourceTitle: Inyo Pools — Motor Shuts Down (bad bearings overheat the motor and trip the overload until it cools)

tips.mechanism: A test that reads only total chlorine can show a healthy number on a pool with no working sanitizer. At 0.2 ppm free and 2.8 ppm combined, a total-only strip returns roughly 3 ppm and looks fine while nothing is being sanitized. This is the mechanism behind 'my strips say chlorine is fine but the pool went green' — the strip answered a different question.
tips.appliesTo: Free vs total vs combined chlorine, test strips vs drop kit, chlorine will not hold
tips._note: Arithmetic of the FC/CC/TC relationship plus strip labeling. Source against a Taylor or LaMotte testing guide in a research session.

tips.mechanism: Open the pool while the water is still below roughly 60F rather than when you want to swim. Algae is close to dormant at that temperature, so an early open is a pool you clean rather than one you rescue. Waiting for warm weather means opening a pool that has been incubating under a cover in still water with no sanitizer — a bloom already in progress.
tips.appliesTo: Pool opening, spring startup, seasonal timing
tips._note: Algae growth vs water temperature — source against a university extension or CDC/MAHC reference.

tips.mechanism: Evaporation concentrates hardness, so a West Texas pool gets harder all summer with nothing done wrong. Water leaves as vapor, minerals stay, and every top-up gallon brings more in — a pool filling at 19-22 gpg concentrates twice over. A calcium reading fine in April can be scaling tile by August. No chemical removes it; dilution is the only route, which is a different conversation in a drought year.
tips.appliesTo: Texas and arid-climate regional articles, calcium hardness, scale
tips._note: Hardness figures sourced (PurityMap, Aquatell) but the evaporation-concentration mechanism itself needs an extension or manufacturer source.

tips.mechanism: A clearing pool goes gray before it goes clear. Dead algae loses its color and becomes fine gray particulate, which usually looks worse than the green did — and that is exactly where people stop dosing, with a day of filtering left to run. Gray means the chlorine won and the job is now the filter's.
tips.appliesTo: Green pool water, algae treatment, how long to clear
tips._note: ASSIGNED WHILE UNSOURCED — predates the verified/candidate rule. Needs a readable source or SYM-001 needs a different tip before it goes live.

tips.mechanism: Shaving cream along the pump lid and unions gets sucked in at the exact leak point, marking it visibly.
tips.appliesTo: Air bubbles, pump losing prime

tips.mechanism: A vitamin C tablet held against a stain fades it in seconds if the stain is metal, not organic.
tips.appliesTo: Stain identification

tips.mechanism: Pour alkalinity-lowering acid in one narrow column with the pump off, then wait — lowers TA with less effect on pH.
tips.appliesTo: Lowering TA without dropping pH

tips.mechanism: Chlorine effectiveness is roughly a percentage of CYA; about 7.5% free chlorine to CYA is the working floor.
tips.appliesTo: Chlorine will not hold, still green after shock
tips._note: Reserved for SYM-016 — do not spend elsewhere.

tips.mechanism: Cold water alone makes an AquaRite report low salt with correct salt in the pool.
tips.appliesTo: AquaRite check salt light
tips._note: Verify against Hayward AquaRite service literature — BRD-031.

tips.mechanism: A pressure gauge reading zero at startup is usually a dead gauge, not a dead pump.
tips.appliesTo: Filter pressure low

tips.mechanism: Run the cleaner hose length test before replacing anything on a suction cleaner.
tips.appliesTo: Cleaner not moving

tips.mechanism: Backwash until the sight glass clears, then rinse 20 seconds — skipping rinse sends the first slug of dirt straight back to the pool.
tips.appliesTo: Backwash vs rinse

tips.mechanism: A start capacitor holds charge after power is off. Discharge before touching it.
tips.appliesTo: Pump hums, will not start

tips.mechanism: Bucket test on the step with the pump running versus off separates a pressure-side leak from evaporation.
tips.appliesTo: Pool losing water

tips.mechanism: Salt cell scale comes off in a 4:1 water-to-acid soak; anything stronger eats the plate coating.
tips.appliesTo: Salt cell cleaning

tips.mechanism: Brush black algae with a stainless brush before treating — treatment cannot reach through the protective cap.
tips.appliesTo: Black algae

tips.mechanism: New plaster dust looks exactly like a cloudy water problem for the first three weeks.
tips.appliesTo: New plaster cloudy

tips.mechanism: Sand blowing into the pool is almost always a cracked lateral or standpipe, not worn sand.
tips.appliesTo: Sand in pool
tips._note: Corroborated by In The Swim and Hallmark Pool Supplies — needs one URL logged to promote to verified.

tips.mechanism: Heater and chlorinator flow switches fail closed as often as open — a No Flow message with visible flow points at the switch.
tips.appliesTo: AquaRite no flow, heater LO code
